Need to search first.I've got notes for most of Hosea 2, but the research is incomplete. My tool access ran out partway through, after I had read Enduring Word (David Guzik), Precept Austin (which only reached v. 2), Ellicott's chapter notes on BibleHub (cut off at v. 15), and search previews from BibleHub and StudyLight. As a result:

- **Missing entirely:** Catholic and Orthodox readings, Lutheran sites, Methodist and Pentecostal sites, the NET Bible notes (only one, quoted on Precept Austin), Bible Odyssey, and any prosperity or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
- **Thin:** vv. 10 and 20–22.
- **Unnamed authors:** some BibleHub "commentaries" pages run several commentators together without labels. Where I couldn't see the name, I say "an entry on this page" rather than guess.
- **Tradition labels:** where I name a commentator's church tradition (e.g. Benson as Methodist), that comes from my own background knowledge, not the pages. Please check those labels before publishing.

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Precept Austin says the chapter break is badly placed: v. 1 belongs with 1:10–11. Dropping the "Lo-" ("not") from the children's names turns "Not My People" and "No Mercy" into "My People" and "Shown Mercy." That reverses Israel's covenant status. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-2-commentary
- Precept Austin also quotes Charles Feinberg: this happens when Israel's Messiah stands on the Mount of Olives. It quotes Bob Utley too: the command "Say" points to a certain future restoration. Same URL.
- **Where readers differ:** one entry on BibleHub reads the verse with chapter 1, as a change of language after Israel's restoration. It says others connect it to what follows: the faithful few who never worshipped Baal are told to plead with their mother. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says brothers and sisters will call each other Ammi and Ruhamah once 1:11 is fulfilled. Another entry says Paul applies these words to Christians, Jews and Gentiles alike (Rom 9:24–25), but literally they meant the godly Israelites of Hosea's day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/2-1.htm
- Ellicott: losing the "Lo-" shows that a waking conscience has given the people their privileges back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm

**v. 2**
- The wording is courtroom language. MacArthur, quoted on Precept Austin: God brings charges, and individual Israelites (the "children") are told to accuse the nation (the "mother"). Gomer's literal unfaithfulness pictures Israel's idolatry. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-2-commentary
- The CSB Study Bible, quoted there, calls this the book's first call to repent. It takes the children as ordinary people and the mother as Israel's leaders. Same URL.
- **Divorce or warning?** The ESV Study Bible (quoted there) suggests "not my wife" may be a threat rather than a real divorce, since the warnings that follow assume the marriage still stands. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-2-commentary
  - An entry on BibleHub says she is not a wife "in point of right," but God has not actually divorced her. The Geneva Bible notes say the fault lay with Israel, not God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/2-2.htm
- Guzik: the relationship is broken, but the blessings continue for now. Quoting Hubbard, he says "between her breasts" may mean she bared herself to attract lovers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
- Ellicott: the mother is the nation as a whole and the children are its people. The "whoredoms… from her face" are her shameless idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: God will reduce Israel to the helpless state she was born in, in Egypt and the wilderness. He suggests a link to babies abandoned at birth (compare Ezek 16:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the images build on each other: birth in Egypt, then wilderness, then dry land, then thirst. Like a wronged husband, God takes back every gift. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hosea/2.htm
- Guzik: this is a warning of judgment if she won't turn. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the children stand for individual Israelites, who will face judgment one by one if they don't return. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
- Ellicott: the children share their mother's guilt, because the people are content with the idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: what makes it worse is that she chases her lovers, not they her. She credits idols with gifts that came from God. Today's equivalent is thanking "Fortune" or "Nature" instead of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm
- Guzik: Israel excused her unfaithfulness by pointing to what she got out of it, missing that sin's pleasures pass (Heb 11:25). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: the hedge of thorns makes wandering painful and the wrong paths hard to find. He calls it one of the sweetest expressions of God's love, though it rarely feels that way. "Return to my first husband" is what we say once sin's pleasures run out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
- Pulpit: the Hebrew verbs show she chases eagerly, yet every way is blocked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hosea/2.htm
- Ellicott: vv. 6–7 sum up the rest of the chapter, so that the path of evil becomes a path of thorns. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm
- Brian Bell, quoted on Precept Austin, compares v. 7 to the prodigal son: Luke has a prodigal son, Hosea a prodigal wife. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-2-commentary

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: God's longing here looks ahead to Luke 15. Grain, wine and oil were Canaan's main crops. Israel made God's gifts into Baal images. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm
- Guzik: God kept providing even while she worshipped idols. He imagines Hosea bringing groceries to Gomer's lover's house. Whatever we give an idol, we first received from God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
- Pulpit: refusing to thank the Giver was made worse by using his gifts for Baal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hosea/2.htm
- Homiletics on BibleHub: people still turn God-given wealth and talents against him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/hosea/2.htm

**vv. 9–10**
- Ellicott: God takes back what was misused. The tool was the king of Assyria, Tiglath-pileser, in 734 BC. Her idol-lovers will watch her fall, unable to help. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm
- Guzik: God removes the provision so that, feeling her need, she might turn back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: joy in worship was not wrong in itself, and these feasts are not called sinful as such. He notes that Jeroboam I had set them up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: vine and fig tree stand for owning land and living in peace. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads "testimony" instead of "forest." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm
- Matthew Henry: an enemy will lay the land waste so beasts eat the fruit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hsa/Hsa_002.cfm

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: "Baals" is plural because Baal was worshipped at many local shrines (Baal-Hermon, Baal-Gad and others). "The days of the Baals" means the whole period of Baal worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm
- Guzik: Israel used the wealth of Jeroboam II's reign for idolatry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
- Bell, quoting Wiersbe on Precept Austin: the church can sell itself to the world and still claim to be faithful. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-2-commentary

**v. 14**
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: God doesn't say "drive" or "drag" but "allure." Love's pull is stronger than any force. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
- Ellicott: "therefore" doesn't mean God's kindness results from the sin. Grace turns suffering into discipline. He takes the wilderness to be exile, repeating the wilderness where Israel was first married to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm
- Homiletics: this "therefore" comes from grace. It speaks of restoring both the literal and the spiritual Israel, and pictures any returning prodigal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/hosea/2.htm
- **Different setting:** Chuck Smith (preview only) places this when God protects Israel from the "man of sin" during the Great Tribulation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/2-15.html

**v. 15**
- The usual reading: Achor means "trouble," where Achan was judged (Josh 7). The place of trouble becomes a door of hope.
  - Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
  - Barnes, Constable, Gill and Matthew Henry: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/2-15.html
  - Henry adds that real sorrow for sin opens a door of hope, and the singing is fulfilled in the gospel. Gill applies it to how a believer's conversion gives hope of glory. Same URL.
- Maclaren applies it personally: troubles can become doors of hope, but only once our "Achan" (sinful attachments) is dealt with. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/hosea/the-valley-of-achor.cfm
- **Calvin disagrees:** he thinks the Achan link is a mistake. Achor was simply the fertile plain Israel entered after the wilderness, so the point is a sudden change from want to plenty, "as from death into life." https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol26/htm/ix.xi.htm
- Ellicott: "from there" means once she leaves exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/2.htm
- A BibleHub Q&A article sees Christ in it: Achan's burial pictures judgment, and Christ's resurrection opens the door of hope. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_Valley_of_Achor_important_in_Hosea_2.htm

**v. 16**
- Shared core: "Ishi" (my husband) versus "Baali" (my master, also the god's name).
- Guzik: God wants love, not a fear-based master–slave relationship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
- Benson (Methodist): Ishi is a word of love, Baali one of submission and fear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/2-16.htm
- John Piper (Baptist): one meaning, which he thinks is the main one, is "relate to me as a loving husband, not a harsh owner." https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/call-me-husband-not-baal
- Others stress the idol's name rather than the master idea. The Wycliffe Bible Commentary, quoted on StudyLight, says both words meant husband, but "Baali" was dropped because of the false god. Barnes says Baal was sometimes a title for a husband. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/2-16.html
- Calvin insists the word "Baal" be kept in translation, not softened to "my Lord." https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom26.ix.xvii.html
- Bell (on Precept Austin) notes the two words were used interchangeably, as in 2 Sam 11:26. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-2-commentary

**v. 17**
- Benson: Israel was forbidden to speak idols' names (Exod 23:13), so even the innocent word "Baal" had to go. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/2-16.htm
- Guzik: the Baals wanted master–slave worship, and the LORD does not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/

**v. 18** (views really differ here)
- **Future, literal earth:** Guzik says it will be fulfilled in the millennial earth, though we can taste it now. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
  - A BibleHub Q&A article reads it as a literal future peace between people and animals, linked to Rom 8:19–22. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Hosea_2_18_for_creation.htm
- **Christ and the church:** Barnes says the "day" is Christ's coming, and God renews in Christ the peace of Paradise lost through Adam. The beasts also picture spiritual enemies, and the Christian rests fearless. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/2-18.htm
- **Practical protection:** Clarke says flocks and crops will not be harmed and war will cease. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/2-18.html
  - Calvin: animals were made to be subject to people, and Adam's sin turned them against us. Here that order is restored. Same URL.
  - Matthew Henry: the creatures God used for judgment will no longer harm. Being taken into covenant with God himself is far greater. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hsa/Hsa_002.cfm
- Ellicott: peace outside matches the moral peace within (compare Isa 11:6–9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/2-18.htm

**v. 19**
- GotQuestions: the triple "I will betroth" shows intensity and seriousness, and the bond will never break. https://www.gotquestions.org/I-will-betroth-you-to-me-forever.html
- Guzik: restored on a solid foundation and never broken again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
- Pulpit: she is not taken back as a divorced wife but betrothed as a chaste virgin, so completely has God forgiven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/hosea/2.htm
- **New Covenant readings:** Barnes says the betrothal involves the new covenant of Jer 31:31–32, and the church is "espoused" to Christ in baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/2-19.html
  - Coffman: this is a new marriage to a new people under the New Covenant, not a remarriage to the apostate. Same URL.
  - What appears to be Ellicott's entry links it to humanity's betrothal to God in Christ's incarnation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/2-19.htm
- Bell (on Precept Austin) says Luther called this verse a wedding ring with six precious stones. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-2-commentary

**v. 20**
- An entry on BibleHub (apparently Ellicott's): righteousness and justice set the terms; kindness and mercy follow so she won't be crushed by fear; and "faithfulness" seals it. Benson, quoting Bishop Horsley, takes "know the LORD" as experiencing his goodness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/2-19.htm
- Guzik: it leads to an ever-deeper relationship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/

**vv. 21–22**
- Guzik: when hearts beat in rhythm with God's, he answers prayer (John 15:7) and provides (Matt 6:33). Jezreel ("God scatters" in judgment) becomes "God sows" seed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/

**v. 23** (views really differ here)
- Guzik: all three children's names, first given as judgment, are turned into marks of mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-2/
- Clarke: "sow her" plays on the name Jezreel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/2-23.html
- **About the Gentiles:** Coffman calls it a clear prophecy of Gentiles brought in, as Paul (Rom 9:25–26) and Peter (1 Pet 2:10) use it. Barnes says it was more true of the Gentiles than of Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/2-23.html
  - GotQuestions agrees: Gentiles are grafted in through faith in Christ. https://www.gotquestions.org/Book-of-Hosea.html
- **About Israel, applied by Paul:** Precept Austin says that in its Old Testament setting the verse means Israel's restoration, and Paul applies it to Gentiles without reinterpreting it. It quotes Denney (Paul applies words first about Israel) and Constable (some see a direct fulfilment, others a partial one with full fulfilment still future). https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_925-28
  - Constable on StudyLight: Paul used it for both Jews and Gentiles converted in the Church Age. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/2-23.html
  - Feinberg (v. 1 note) ties the full reversal to Israel at Messiah's return. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-2-commentary

---

**The main split across traditions** shows up at vv. 1, 14, 18–19 and 23:
- **A future, literal restoration of Israel:** Guzik, Feinberg, Chuck Smith, Constable.
- **Fulfilment in Christ and the church:** Barnes, Coffman, Gill, Matthew Henry.

Calvin stands apart on v. 15 (Achor).

To fill the gaps, the next places to check are newadvent.org (Church Fathers on Hosea 2), the netbible.org notes for Hosea 2, and the lcms.org and seedbed.com search pages.
